name: Marco Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Most days start at the kitchen table with a coffee and whatever the agency sent overnight, usually a tenancy contract or a school letter from Italian into English. Two or three mornings a week I'm at the county hospital or the family court on River Street, interpreting for Italian families who can't follow what's being said. I like the court work best, because you can see it matters to someone. What wears me out is the chasing: invoices, the agency's portal, and the rates that never go up.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said the rates never go up. What does a month look like, money-wise?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: In a good month I clear just enough for my half of the rent with Lena, my partner, and the bills, and there's maybe a hundred left. In a bad month I dip into the overdraft. There are only two agencies within an hour of here that do Italian, so if one drops me, there's not much else to go to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, and I'd mean it. I'd tell the people at the translators' association meeting that this proves what we've been saying: you can't replace a person who understands what a frightened mother in a courtroom actually means. Online I'd probably share something smug about the bubble bursting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it doesn't fix my real problem. The agencies already send me machine-translated text and pay me a third less to 'just tidy it up', and that wouldn't stop because AI stalled. My rent still goes up every spring, and I still have less than one month saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am, the same two agencies and the same hospital and court bookings. I'd push the association to fight for a minimum rate for public-service interpreting, because that's where the squeeze really is. Maybe I'd ask Lena if we could find a cheaper flat when the lease ends in August.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, but only for about a day. Then it's the same tight feeling I have now every time the electricity bill comes in. It's not dramatic, it's just a low worry that never quite leaves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the agency paying a third less for tidying up machine text. Do you take those jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I turned the first few down out of principle. Then February came and I took them, because principle doesn't pay the gas. I hate them, honestly; you spend longer fixing a sentence that's almost right than writing your own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing radical changes, what does next year look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as this one, a bit poorer. Prices rise, my rate doesn't, and I keep telling myself I'll do the court interpreter exam that pays better. The exam costs money I don't have, which is the joke of it.

say: This proves a **human interpreter** can't be swapped for software.
The AI hype was always about **cutting our pay**, not about better work.
think: My real problem is **agency rates**, and those keep falling with or without smarter AI.
With under **one month saved**, I'm only ever one lost client from trouble.
do: Keep the same **two agencies** and the hospital and court bookings.
Push the **translators' association** to fight for a minimum public-service rate.
Ask Lena about a **cheaper flat** when the lease ends in August.
feel: **Relieved** for a day, then back to the usual low worry about bills.
S0.quote: I turned the first few down out of principle. Then February came and I took them, because principle doesn't pay the gas.
fieldNote: Even with AI stalled, his **income squeeze** is already here through agency post-editing rates.
Strong **union instinct**: he frames everything as a fight over rates, not technology.
He admits taking the cut-price jobs he says he **opposes**; money beats principle.

steps.text: Keep the two Italian agencies and the court and hospital bookings
Bring a public-service minimum rate motion to the translators' association
Look for a cheaper flat with Lena when the lease ends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: this is a choice companies are making, not the weather. I'd post that the courts and hospitals should be legally required to use qualified human interpreters, and I'd sign every petition going. At the association I'd want us to stop being polite about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the document side of my work disappears. Contracts and school letters are exactly the 'writing and checking' that card is talking about, and that's about half my income. The court and hospital work might hold for a while, but councils love cutting interpreting budgets, so I don't trust it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd finally sit the court interpreter exam, even if it means borrowing the fee from my brother. I'd ask the hospital for more regular shifts so I'm less dependent on the agency. And I'd go to every association meeting and get people to write to the health board about keeping human interpreters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. I picked this because I loved languages, and I'd be watching it get turned into a cheap button. Angry too, which is easier than being scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd borrow the exam fee from your brother. How would that conversation go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly at first. My brother Paolo works in a warehouse and thinks I chose a hobby, not a job. He'd lend it, but I'd have to hear about it at every family lunch for a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've never used these AI tools yourself. Would you try them if that's where the work went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I really don't want to. It feels like training my own replacement. If the agency made it the only way to get jobs, I'd probably have to, but I'd do the bare minimum and I'd hate every minute.

say: Replacing interpreters is a **choice companies make**, not something that just happens.
Courts and hospitals should be **legally required** to use qualified humans.
think: About **half my income** comes from documents, and that part is going.
I don't trust **council budgets** to protect the court and hospital work for long.
do: Sit the **court interpreter exam**, borrowing the fee from his brother.
Ask the hospital for **regular shifts** to depend less on the agency.
Organise association members to write to the **health board**.
feel: **Sick and angry** watching something he loves become a cheap button.
Anger feels easier to hold than the **fear** underneath it.
S1.quote: I picked this because I loved languages, and I'd be watching it get turned into a cheap button.
fieldNote: He expects to lose **half his income** quickly, which he states plainly.
His plan is to move into **protected human work**, court and hospital, rather than learn the tools.
Resistance is emotional: using AI feels like **training his replacement**.

steps.text: Sit the court interpreter exam with a loan from his brother
Ask the county hospital for a regular weekly interpreting shift
Get association members writing to the health board about human interpreters
Borrow the exam fee from his brother Paolo

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment governments either protect people or they don't, and we'd find out which very fast. I'd be at whatever protest there was. Online I'd be the angry one sharing every story about people losing work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm finished as a translator within a year of it arriving, maybe sooner. The thinking part is my whole job; there's no hands-on bit to hide in. The robots coming three years later doesn't help me at all, except that it means hands-on jobs would still be open for a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know. I'd keep taking whatever court bookings were left. I'd probably ask my uncle about the delivery firm he drives for, because a van would still need a driver for a while. And I'd sign on for whatever support the government offered, without any shame about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor's gone. I've got no savings, no plan and two years isn't enough to retrain into anything that pays. I'd be lying awake doing sums that don't work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the robots coming three years later doesn't help you. Can you say more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My whole job happens in my head and in my mouth. A robot is a delivery van or a care worker's arms; that's not what replaces me. AGI replaces me on the first day, and the three years only matter if I jump into a job with my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Lena on the night it was announced?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Lena that her nursery job is probably safer than mine for once, and that we'd need to live on her wage for a bit. That would sting. She'd say it's fine, and I'd know she was worried too.

say: Governments will show very fast whether they'll **protect people** or not.
I'd be at the **protests** and sharing every story of people losing work.
think: I'm **finished as a translator** within a year; my job is all thinking.
The three-year **robot delay** only helps if I jump into hands-on work.
do: Take whatever **court bookings** remain while they last.
Ask his uncle about **van driving** at the delivery firm.
Claim **government support** straight away, without shame.
feel: The **floor has gone**: no savings, no plan, no time to retrain.
S2.quote: AGI replaces me on the first day, and the three years only matter if I jump into a job with my hands.
fieldNote: He sees clearly that the **robot delay** offers nothing to purely thinking work.
With no cushion and two years, he has **no workable plan**, only stopgaps.
He'd lean on **Lena's wage** and public support, and finds that painful.

steps.text: Ask his uncle for van driving work at the delivery firm
Apply for government income support as soon as it opens
March with the association at the first protest for human interpreters

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message, but with more time to organise: let's get laws in place before it lands. I'd say we need a guaranteed income or retraining paid for by the companies making money from this. I'd say it in the association's newsletter, not just on social media.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to see my document work drain away bit by bit. I think by 2029 I'd be living off court and hospital bookings only. It's still the same ending for me, just slower and with time to hate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first year doing the court exam and pushing for a law that says a qualified human must interpret in court. In year two or three I'd look seriously at something hands-on, maybe training as a care worker, since the robots come later there. Lena's mum is a care manager, so she could point me somewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still scared, but it's a scared I can do something with. I'd have a list of things to try, which matters. It's the sitting still I can't stand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really go into care work? It's a long way from languages.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's not that far, honestly. Half my hospital jobs are sitting with an old Italian man who's scared and can't understand the nurse. I'd still be talking to people; I'd just be lifting them too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the court exam actually get you, if AI arrives by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe three or four years of better-paid work before it goes. The court exam isn't a career, it's a bridge. A few years of better pay keeps the rent covered while I train for the next thing.

say: Let's get **laws in place** before it lands, not after.
Companies profiting should pay for **guaranteed income** or retraining.
think: My **document work** drains away and I'm left with court and hospital bookings.
It's the **same ending**, just slower and with time to hate it.
do: Pass the **court exam** in year one and campaign for human court interpreting.
Train as a **care worker** in years two or three, using Lena's mum's contacts.
feel: **Scared**, but with a list of things to try, which helps.
Can't stand **sitting still** while it comes.
S3.quote: The court exam isn't a career, it's a bridge. A few years of better pay keeps the rent covered while I train for the next thing.
fieldNote: The extra time turns panic into a **two-step plan**: court work, then care work.
He links care work to his **hospital interpreting**, which makes the jump believable.
Still expects to **lose his trade**; only the timing changes.

steps.text: Pass the court interpreter exam in the first year
Campaign for a law requiring human interpreters in court
Start a care worker course through Lena's mum's contacts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it, and a waste if we let companies decide everything. I'd want the association to work with the nurses' and care unions, because they're the ones who'll still have members. Publicly I'd sound almost hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years takes me to 37, which is a lot of my working life left with no trade. But it's long enough to build something else properly instead of panicking. I'd probably still be translating for three or four of those years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the court and hospital work going and do the exam. I'd save, even fifty a month, which I've never managed. By year three or four I'd start a proper nursing or care qualification part-time, and I'd keep pushing the association to fight for retraining money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but it's a slower worry. I can picture getting through it, which I can't with the fast ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said fifty a month. Where would that come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably from the car. It takes forty minutes longer, but cancelling the car and taking the bus to the court is fifty-five a month in insurance and fuel. That's my savings plan, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you dislike AI tools. Over ten years, does that change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little. If I'm going into care, I'd use whatever the hospital uses, because that's a tool for helping people, not for replacing me. I'd still never use it to translate.

say: **Ten years** is a gift if we use it and a waste if companies decide.
Translators should team up with **nurses' and care unions**.
think: At **37** I'd have plenty of working life left with no trade.
There's time to **build something** properly instead of panicking.
do: Keep **court and hospital** interpreting going for three or four years.
Save **fifty a month** by selling the car and taking the bus.
Start a **part-time nursing** or care qualification by year four.
feel: **Worried**, but a slower worry he can picture getting through.
S4.quote: Cancelling the car and taking the bus to the court is fifty-five a month in insurance and fuel. That's my savings plan, really.
fieldNote: The decade gives him a **real plan** and his first ever savings habit.
His tool resistance softens only for **care work**, never for translation.
He keeps the **union framing** throughout, now aimed at alliances.

steps.text: Keep court and hospital interpreting for the next three or four years
Sell the car and save fifty a month
Enrol in a part-time nursing qualification by year four
Push the association to join forces with the care workers' union

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. Two years with no savings and a job that's all thinking, I'd have nothing to stand on. What would help is a law that keeps qualified humans in courts and hospitals, and someone paying for retraining so I don't have to borrow from my brother.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the people I interpret for. If the machine gets a word wrong at a custody hearing, a family loses a child. Nobody's asking those families what they want.

headlineQuote: If the machine gets a word wrong at a custody hearing, a family loses a child. Nobody's asking those families what they want.
portrait: Marco is a **27-year-old** Italian–English freelance interpreter and translator living with his partner Lena.
He earns little, has **under a month** saved and depends on two local agencies.
He never uses AI and sees it as **training his replacement**.
His answer is always **collective**: union fights, laws for human interpreters, public support.
Faster AGI leaves him **panicked**; with ten years he builds a path into care work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his work is all thinking and he has no savings to fall back on.
whatWouldHelp: A **law** keeping qualified humans in courts and hospitals.
**Paid retraining** so he doesn't have to borrow from family.
